messages.content: I want to develop a semantic parser that generalizes variable binding and quantifier scope to unseen compositions without sacrificing accuracy on familiar constructions. What would make that goal precise?

The goal has two requirements. On withheld scope–binding combinations, with matched vocabulary and length distributions, the parser should achieve at least 90% logical-form exact match. On familiar constructions, its exact-match accuracy should remain within two percentage points of an equally sized supervised baseline. Both matter: success on unfamiliar combinations should not come at the expense of the familiar ones.
Why mention variable binding and quantifier scope together?

They are related aspects of meaning that can interact. Variable binding concerns which expression a variable is associated with; quantifier scope concerns how quantified expressions are ordered in a logical interpretation. The goal is not merely to handle each aspect in isolation, but to handle scope–binding combinations the parser has not seen before.
So does “unseen” mean the test uses unfamiliar words?

Not necessarily. The requirement specifically concerns withheld scope–binding combinations with matched vocabulary and length distributions. That directs attention to generalization across combinations, rather than treating unfamiliar vocabulary or a different length distribution as the defining challenge.
Does matching the length distribution mean every withheld input has a familiar input of exactly the same length?

The stated condition is about matched length distributions. It does not, by itself, require a one-to-one length match for every input. Likewise, matched vocabulary does not by itself say that every individual input contains exactly the same words as another input.
What is the significance of logical-form exact match here?

It makes the target a full logical-form match, rather than credit for getting only part of an interpretation right. For this requirement, the threshold is at least 90% exact match on the withheld scope–binding combinations. The node does not specify additional conventions for representing or comparing logical forms, so those should not be assumed.
Would 90% count, or does it need to be higher?
Exactly 90% meets a requirement written as “≥90%.” A score below 90% would not meet that threshold.
And the other number is two percent?

It is two percentage points, not a two-percent relative change. The comparison is between familiar-construction exact-match accuracy and the accuracy of an equally sized supervised baseline; the goal is to keep them within two percentage points.
What should I take “equally sized” to specify?

It qualifies the supervised baseline used for the familiar-construction comparison. The goal does not say what aspect of size is being matched, so it is best to retain the phrase “equally sized supervised baseline” rather than assume a particular model size, training-set size, or other definition.
Is the familiar-construction condition secondary to the withheld-combination result?

No. The two requirements jointly express the goal. Reaching at least 90% logical-form exact match on the withheld combinations would not, on its own, establish that familiar-construction accuracy was maintained within two percentage points of the equally sized supervised baseline.
Could the parser do well on familiar constructions but still miss the point?

Yes. Familiar-construction accuracy alone would not demonstrate generalization to the withheld scope–binding combinations. The goal calls for both strong exact-match performance on those unseen compositions and accuracy close to the specified baseline on familiar constructions.
I’m trying to distinguish learning the pieces from handling their combinations. Is that a fair way to read it?

Yes, as a conceptual reading. The emphasis is on whether variable binding and quantifier scope work together in combinations that were withheld, not merely whether the parser recognizes the relevant elements separately. The matched vocabulary and length distributions help state that target without making new words or a length shift part of the requirement.
Does the goal prescribe a particular parser design or training method?

No. It states the capability to develop and the two accuracy requirements. It does not select an architecture, a training procedure, or an explanation for why a parser might meet or miss either requirement.
Should I describe either threshold as an achieved result?

No. These are targets for the semantic parser, not reported outcomes. The precise statement is that it should achieve ≥90% logical-form exact match on the specified withheld combinations and keep familiar-construction exact-match accuracy within two percentage points of the equally sized supervised baseline.
So the concise version is: generalize scope and binding to unseen combinations under the matched vocabulary and length conditions, while retaining familiar accuracy relative to that baseline?

Yes. To keep the concise version fully precise, include both numerical conditions: at least 90% logical-form exact match on withheld scope–binding combinations with matched vocabulary and length distributions, and familiar-construction exact-match accuracy within two percentage points of an equally sized supervised baseline.

For the scope-and-binding goal, I want to propose training ScopeBind to decode alpha-normalized logical forms through binder-link and scope-permutation actions, using counterfactual recombination plus familiar-example rehearsal. How should I understand the pieces of that proposal?

It proposes both a way for ScopeBind to produce logical forms and a way to train it. The decoding side uses actions concerned with binder links and scope permutations, with alpha-normalized logical forms as the output. The training side combines counterfactual recombination with rehearsal on familiar examples. Those are proposed means of addressing the goal, not a claim that the accuracy targets have already been met.
What does alpha-normalized mean in this setting?

It concerns the names of bound variables. Two logical forms can differ only because their bound variables have different names, while expressing the same binding relationships. Alpha-normalization puts such naming on a consistent footing. It does not make genuinely different binder links or different quantifier scopes equivalent.
So normalization is not meant to hide a scope error?

Right. Renaming a bound variable and changing which quantifier takes scope are different operations. Alpha-normalization addresses the former; the proposed scope-permutation actions address the latter. A change in which binder an occurrence is linked to is likewise substantive, rather than a mere change of variable name.
What work are the binder-link actions supposed to do?

At a conceptual level, they express which binder a variable occurrence belongs to. That makes a binding relationship an explicit part of producing the logical form, rather than relying solely on the final spelling of variable names. The proposal does not specify the actions’ exact encoding or the order in which they must be emitted.
And a scope-permutation action is about the ordering of quantifiers?

Yes. It represents the scope-ordering aspect of the logical form. The point of distinguishing it from a binder-link action is that the two capture different relationships: one concerns how quantified expressions are scoped, and the other concerns which occurrences are bound by which binders. Both can matter in the same interpretation.
Why describe these as decoding actions instead of simply saying that ScopeBind outputs a logical form?

“Outputs a logical form” states the end product. The proposal is more specific about how that product is to be decoded: through binder-link and scope-permutation actions, yielding an alpha-normalized logical form. That description identifies the relationships the decoding process is meant to express without committing to an unspecified architecture or action syntax.
Could alpha-normalization, by itself, give the generalization we want?

The proposal does not establish that it could. Alpha-normalization can remove variation due solely to bound-variable names, but unseen scope–binding combinations still require the parser to handle the relevant relationships together. That is why the proposal also names binder-link and scope-permutation actions and a training approach.
What does counterfactual recombination contribute, at least as an idea?

As an idea, it is meant to put components into recombined configurations so ScopeBind has a reason to learn how binding and scope behave across combinations, rather than only reproducing familiar combinations. The node does not give a specific recipe for constructing those counterfactuals, or say which recombinations would be used.
Would it be accurate to say the counterfactual examples are already known to be effective?

No. Counterfactual recombination is part of the proposed training approach. Nothing here reports a training outcome or establishes that it is effective. Its intended role is understandable from the goal, but whether the proposed approach meets that goal remains open.
What is the role of familiar-example rehearsal alongside that recombination?

It keeps familiar examples present in the proposed training approach. That aligns with the requirement not to sacrifice familiar-construction accuracy while pursuing generalization to withheld combinations. The proposal does not specify how much rehearsal to use, how to schedule it, or what accuracy it produces.
Is it fair to think of those two training elements as addressing different sides of the goal?

Yes, as a description of their intended roles. Counterfactual recombination speaks to learning across new scope–binding combinations; familiar-example rehearsal speaks to retaining performance on familiar constructions. The proposal combines them rather than treating generalization and familiar accuracy as interchangeable.
I do not want to imply that binder-link actions alone determine scope. Is that distinction clear enough?

It is worth keeping explicit. A binder link says which binder is associated with an occurrence; scope concerns the relative reach or ordering of quantified expressions. The proposal names both binder-link and scope-permutation actions because specifying one kind of relationship is not the same as specifying the other.
Does the proposal say whether these actions are generated in separate stages?

No. It says ScopeBind would decode via both kinds of actions, but it does not specify separate stages, a fixed action order, or whether one kind must be completed before the other. Those would be additional implementation choices, not facts supplied by this proposal.
How does the proposed output relate to logical-form exact match?

The intended output is an alpha-normalized logical form, and the goal evaluates logical-form exact match. Normalizing variable names can clarify the distinction between superficial renaming and meaningful differences in binding or scope. The proposal does not specify the full evaluation convention, however, so it should not be read as changing the stated exact-match requirement.
Can I connect this back to the numerical targets without claiming success?

Yes. You can say that ScopeBind is proposed as a way to pursue at least 90% logical-form exact match on withheld scope–binding combinations with matched vocabulary and length distributions, while keeping familiar-construction exact-match accuracy within two percentage points of an equally sized supervised baseline. Those are the goal’s requirements, not measured results for ScopeBind.
Does familiar-example rehearsal guarantee the comparison with the baseline?

No. Rehearsal is a proposed means of attending to familiar constructions during training. The requirement remains an accuracy comparison against an equally sized supervised baseline, and the proposal provides no result showing that the comparison is satisfied.
Could I specify a particular source for the recombined examples when restating this?

Not as though it were already part of the proposal. “Counterfactual recombination” is specified, but the source of examples and the procedure for recombining them are not. A faithful restatement can name the method without filling in those missing details.
Then give me a compact statement that keeps the method and its status straight.

Propose training ScopeBind to decode alpha-normalized logical forms using binder-link and scope-permutation actions, with counterfactual recombination and familiar-example rehearsal. The approach is intended to support generalization to unseen scope–binding combinations while maintaining familiar-construction accuracy; no performance result is asserted.
How should ScopeBind filter counterfactual recombinations that violate binder accessibility under nested quantifier scopes?

A possible approach is to validate each proposed recombination against the scope structure it creates: for every variable occurrence with a binder link, ask whether that binder’s scope actually contains the occurrence. If a recombination moves an occurrence outside the scope of its linked binder, or changes the nesting so that the link is no longer licensed, it would fail that check. This is a candidate filtering principle, not a specified procedure for ScopeBind.
Can you clarify what “accessible” means here without assuming a particular implementation?

In the ordinary nested-scope sense, a binder is accessible to an occurrence when the occurrence falls within the portion of the logical form governed by that binder. Merely having a binder somewhere in the form is insufficient. The relevant question is about the relationship between the occurrence, its intended binder link, and the resulting scope boundaries—not simply whether their variable names happen to match.
Would alpha-normalizing the recombined logical form catch an inaccessible binder link?

Not by itself. Alpha-normalization makes bound-variable naming consistent; it cannot put an occurrence back inside a binder’s scope. An accessibility check would need to examine the binding and scope relationships represented by the recombination. Renaming is not a substitute for checking those relationships.
Suppose a scope-permutation action changes the nesting but leaves the binder links untouched. Is that the kind of case the question is about?

Yes, that is a useful general illustration. A link that was coherent under one nesting should not simply be presumed coherent under a different nesting. After the proposed scope permutation, the link would need to be checked against the new scope boundaries. That does not mean every permutation invalidates a link; it means accessibility has to be assessed for the resulting combination.
Would checking for a matching variable name be enough?

No. Bound-variable names can be changed without changing the binding structure, and the same written name does not, on its own, establish that an occurrence is within the intended binder’s scope. Since ScopeBind is proposed to use binder-link actions, the natural conceptual check is whether each link is licensed by the resulting nested scope structure.
Can you give a small illustration of a violation?

Imagine a candidate logical form with an occurrence linked to a quantifier that governs only an inner region, while the occurrence sits outside that region. Under that nesting, the quantifier cannot bind that occurrence. The illustration is about relative scope and position; the particular words or variable names are incidental.
What about an occurrence inside an inner quantifier’s scope that links to an outer binder?

Under an ordinary nested-binder interpretation, being inside an inner scope does not automatically make an outer binder inaccessible. The check should concern whether the linked outer binder still governs that occurrence in the resulting form, rather than rejecting a link merely because another quantifier is nested between them. Any more restrictive rule would need to be specified separately.
So a filter based only on how many quantifiers intervene could reject legitimate recombinations?

It could. The number of intervening quantifiers is not the same thing as accessibility. What matters conceptually is whether the occurrence remains in the scope of the binder identified by its link after the recombination establishes its nesting.
At what point would this check happen—before or after the recombination?

The violation is defined with respect to the structure the recombination produces, so that resulting structure must be considered when judging accessibility. One possible workflow would check each candidate before treating it as a usable training example. The question does not specify ScopeBind’s generation workflow, though, so it does not settle an exact validation stage.
Does this mean every candidate with a questionable link must be thrown away, or could its link be changed?

Those are distinct possible design choices. Rejecting a candidate would filter out the inaccessible link; changing the link would produce a different candidate that would need its own validity check and intended interpretation. The question asks how to filter violating recombinations, but it does not decide whether repair is permitted or how a repaired example would be labeled.
If a repaired example has a valid binder link, can it be treated as the original counterfactual example?

Not automatically. Changing a binder link can change the logical form’s meaning, even if the revised link is accessible. Structural validity and preservation of the intended counterfactual interpretation are separate questions. The supplied proposal does not give a rule for deciding whether such a revision still serves the intended recombination.
Is a scope-permutation action itself enough to tell us whether all links are accessible?

It describes a scope relationship, but accessibility also depends on where the variable occurrences are and which binders their links identify. Considering the permutation and binder links together is the important point. The proposal names both action types, without specifying a built-in validity check between them.
Could the filter just verify that the final logical form is alpha-normalized?

That would check a different property. An alpha-normalized form can still contain a binder link that is not licensed by its nested scopes. A filter aimed at binder accessibility would have to assess that relationship explicitly, rather than rely on the form’s naming convention.
Would you state the rule as “keep every recombination whose variables are bound”?

That is too broad for this question. A candidate might appear to have a binder identified for every occurrence, yet an identified binder might not be accessible under the candidate’s scope nesting. A more targeted principle is to check each proposed binder link against the scope structure produced by the recombination.
Does this question already establish the precise accessibility formalism ScopeBind uses?

No. It identifies the problem—counterfactual recombinations that violate binder accessibility under nested quantifier scopes—but does not define a formal scope representation, a complete validity algorithm, or rules for exceptional cases. The containment-style check we have discussed is a general way to frame the issue, not a claim that those details have been fixed.
How should I phrase the question so it stays open but still points to a concrete concern?

You could ask: “When ScopeBind counterfactually recombines binder links and quantifier-scope orderings, how can it identify and filter candidates whose resulting nested scopes make a proposed binder inaccessible to its linked variable occurrence?” That keeps the focus on the resulting scope–binding relationship without presupposing a particular filtering algorithm.
And this is a question about the proposed training examples, not a claim about performance?

Correct. It asks how to handle a potential validity issue in counterfactual recombination. It does not report that ScopeBind has been trained, that a filter has been selected, or that either of the goal’s accuracy requirements has been achieved.

My hypothesis is that filtering ScopeBind’s counterfactual recombinations by scope-tree dominance and binder-type compatibility will achieve ≥90% withheld exact match without exceeding a two-point familiar-accuracy deficit. How should I state that carefully?

State it as a prediction, not a result: filtering counterfactual recombinations by both scope-tree dominance and binder-type compatibility is hypothesized to yield at least 90% exact match on the withheld scope–binding combinations, while keeping the familiar-construction accuracy deficit at no more than two percentage points relative to the equally sized supervised baseline. Neither outcome is established by the hypothesis itself.
What does scope-tree dominance contribute to the proposed filter?

Conceptually, it checks the scope relationship between a proposed binder and the occurrence linked to it. If the binder’s scope does not encompass that occurrence in the recombined structure, the link fails an accessibility check. Expressing that relationship through scope-tree dominance gives the filter a way to consider the resulting nesting rather than just the presence of a binder somewhere in the logical form.
And what is binder-type compatibility meant to check?

It is a separate compatibility condition on the proposed binder link: the binder and what it is proposed to bind must be compatible under the applicable binder types. The hypothesis names that condition but does not define the type system or the exact compatibility rule, so it would be premature to specify particular types or claim that a particular pair passes.
Is the hypothesis saying to use either condition, or both?
Both. It proposes filtering by scope-tree dominance and binder-type compatibility. A candidate that satisfies only one of the two would not satisfy the combined criterion as stated.
Suppose a proposed binder dominates an occurrence in the scope tree, but the types are incompatible. Would the filter retain it?

Under the proposed two-condition filter, no. Dominance would address the scope relationship, but it would not override a failure of binder-type compatibility. That is a conceptual consequence of requiring both checks, not a report about a particular example.
What if the types are compatible but the binder does not dominate the occurrence?
That would fail the dominance condition. Type compatibility cannot make an occurrence accessible to a binder whose scope does not reach it in the recombined structure.
Does the hypothesis claim that these two checks catch every possible problem with a recombined logical form?

No. It specifies two filtering criteria and predicts an accuracy outcome from using them. It does not assert that the criteria constitute a complete validity test for every possible logical-form issue.
Could I say the filter guarantees valid training examples?

That would go beyond the hypothesis. You can say it is intended to filter recombinations on the stated dominance and compatibility grounds. A guarantee that every retained example is valid would require more than the hypothesis provides.
How is this an answer to the question about binder accessibility under nested scopes?

Scope-tree dominance addresses whether the proposed binder has the necessary scope relationship to its linked occurrence after recombination. Binder-type compatibility adds a second constraint on that proposed link. Together, they offer a specific filtering hypothesis for the accessibility problem, while leaving its predicted effect on accuracy to be established.
Does “will achieve ≥90%” sound too certain for a hypothesis?

It is appropriate as the outcome the hypothesis predicts, provided it is clearly attributed to the hypothesis. For example, “The hypothesis predicts that this filtering will achieve ≥90% withheld exact match.” It should not be phrased as though a measured score of ≥90% already exists.
When I say “withheld exact match,” what is withheld?

In the stated goal, the withheld items are scope–binding combinations, evaluated by logical-form exact match with matched vocabulary and length distributions. The hypothesis’s ≥90% prediction is about that withheld-combination accuracy, not an unspecified accuracy measure on all inputs.
And is “two-point deficit” a relative percentage drop?

No. Here it means a deficit of no more than two percentage points in familiar-construction exact-match accuracy relative to the equally sized supervised baseline. It is not a two-percent relative decrease.
If the deficit is exactly two percentage points, does that satisfy the prediction?

Yes. “Without exceeding a two-point deficit” includes a deficit of exactly two percentage points. Likewise, exactly 90% meets the “≥90%” withheld exact-match threshold. The hypothesis predicts meeting both conditions.
Does the familiar-accuracy part follow automatically if the filter improves the withheld score?

No. The prediction has two distinct parts: a threshold for withheld exact match and a limit on the familiar-accuracy deficit. Improvement on withheld combinations would not by itself establish that familiar-construction accuracy stays within the stated limit.
Should I attribute the familiar-accuracy prediction specifically to familiar-example rehearsal?

Not as a claim made by this hypothesis. The ScopeBind proposal includes familiar-example rehearsal, but this hypothesis specifically predicts what filtering recombinations by scope-tree dominance and binder-type compatibility will accomplish. It does not isolate the contribution of rehearsal or assign the familiar-accuracy outcome to one component.
Could the filter be described as changing ScopeBind’s decoding actions?

The hypothesis concerns filtering counterfactual recombinations, not a change to the proposed binder-link and scope-permutation decoding actions. Those actions provide context for why binder relationships and scope order matter, but a modified decoding procedure is not part of this hypothesis.
Does alpha-normalization replace either filtering check?

No. Alpha-normalization concerns consistent naming of bound variables in logical forms. It does not, by itself, establish that a binder dominates an occurrence in the recombined scope tree or that their types are compatible.
If a recombination fails a check, does the hypothesis require repairing it rather than excluding it?

It says to filter recombinations by the two criteria, but it does not specify a repair procedure. You need not imply that a failing candidate is rewritten, relinked, or otherwise converted into a different example.
Can I call scope-tree dominance a proof that a particular binder link is correct?

Not on its own. It can address whether the proposed link satisfies a scope relationship. Binder-type compatibility is also part of the hypothesized filter, and even passing both checks is not presented here as proof that a particular logical form is the intended interpretation.
So the testable claim is about accuracy after applying the proposed filtering, not just about rejecting inaccessible candidates?

Exactly. The proposed criteria describe what the filter examines. The hypothesis goes further by predicting two outcomes for ScopeBind: ≥90% logical-form exact match on the withheld scope–binding combinations and no more than a two-percentage-point familiar-construction accuracy deficit against the equally sized supervised baseline. Those predicted outcomes remain to be measured.
Give me one sentence that includes the filtering rule and both thresholds without sounding like a completed experiment.

We hypothesize that filtering ScopeBind’s counterfactual recombinations by scope-tree dominance and binder-type compatibility will yield ≥90% logical-form exact match on withheld scope–binding combinations with matched vocabulary and length distributions, while keeping familiar-construction exact-match accuracy no more than two percentage points below that of an equally sized supervised baseline.

I want to turn the filtering idea into a plan: generate ScopeBind recombinations, filter them by scope-tree dominance and binder type, then compare withheld and familiar exact match against a supervised baseline. Is that the right sequence?

Yes. The plan has three stated parts: generate the recombinations, apply both filtering criteria, and compare exact-match accuracy on withheld and familiar constructions against the supervised baseline. It describes work to do, not results already obtained.
What makes the first step more than simply collecting familiar examples?

It calls for generating ScopeBind recombinations. In the proposed approach, recombination is the way to consider new arrangements of scope and binding, rather than only familiar arrangements. The plan does not specify a generation procedure or a number of recombinations.
Should filtering happen with respect to the scope structure of each resulting recombination?

That is the relevant structure for the proposed dominance check. The question is whether a proposed binder has the required scope relationship to the occurrence linked to it in the recombination as generated. The plan names scope-tree dominance as a criterion but does not specify a formal test for applying it.
What does binder type add to that check?

It adds a compatibility check that is distinct from scope-tree dominance. A proposed link can satisfy the relevant scope relationship without necessarily satisfying the binder-type condition. The plan calls for filtering by both, without defining the types or the precise compatibility rules.
If a recombination passes the type check but fails dominance, is it still filtered?

Yes, under a filter that requires both stated criteria. Passing the binder-type check does not make a binder accessible when the required scope-tree relationship fails. Conversely, passing dominance does not remove the need to check binder type.
Does this plan settle whether a failed recombination is discarded or repaired?
No. It says to filter by scope-tree dominance and binder type. It does not give a repair rule or say that an altered recombination should be substituted for one that fails a check.
Do I need to say that the filter proves every retained logical form is correct?

No. The stated checks concern particular scope and binder-type conditions. Passing them should not be presented as proof that a retained recombination is the intended interpretation, or as a complete guarantee about every aspect of its logical form.
The last step says to compare both withheld and familiar exact match against the supervised baseline. Should I preserve both comparisons explicitly?

Yes. The plan calls for comparing withheld exact match and familiar exact match against the supervised baseline. Leaving either one out would narrow the stated comparison. The established goal also gives each evaluation a distinct role: a ≥90% logical-form exact-match target for withheld scope–binding combinations, and a familiar-construction exact-match accuracy limit relative to an equally sized supervised baseline.
Does the ≥90% target itself replace the withheld comparison against the baseline?

No. The ≥90% target is an absolute threshold for withheld scope–binding combinations with matched vocabulary and length distributions. This plan additionally says to compare withheld exact match against the supervised baseline. Those are different ways of examining the withheld result, and neither is a result yet.
And what exactly is the familiar-construction limit?

The goal is to keep familiar-construction exact-match accuracy within two percentage points of an equally sized supervised baseline. That is a percentage-point comparison, not a two-percent relative change. The plan’s familiar comparison provides a way to examine that requirement; it does not establish that the limit is met.
Should I describe the comparison as one combined exact-match score?

No. The plan distinguishes withheld and familiar exact match. Keeping them distinct makes it possible to see performance on unseen scope–binding combinations and performance on familiar constructions, rather than obscuring either in a single combined figure.
Can I say that the supervised baseline is equally sized?

Yes, that qualifier is part of the established familiar-construction requirement. It is safest to call it an “equally sized supervised baseline” without assuming which aspect of size is matched; the plan does not settle that detail.
Is the plan asserting that the filtered recombinations will hit the hypothesis’s predicted accuracy?

No. It sets out generation, filtering, and comparison. The prediction of ≥90% withheld exact match without more than a two-percentage-point familiar-accuracy deficit remains a hypothesis. The comparison is how those outcomes would be examined, not evidence that they have occurred.
Where does ScopeBind’s alpha-normalized decoding fit in this statement?

It identifies the proposed parser approach to which the plan belongs, but this plan’s new steps are generating recombinations, filtering them by scope-tree dominance and binder type, and comparing exact-match performance. You need not restate or change the binder-link and scope-permutation decoding proposal to express this plan.
Does the plan specify how much familiar-example rehearsal to use?

No. Familiar-example rehearsal is part of the ScopeBind proposal, but this plan does not set an amount or schedule for it. The familiar exact-match comparison remains important regardless of those unspecified details.
If I say ‘filter inaccessible binders,’ would that capture the whole filtering step?

It captures the accessibility concern behind the dominance criterion, but it omits binder type. A faithful statement of this plan should name both scope-tree dominance and binder type rather than compressing them into accessibility alone.
Could I replace ‘scope-tree dominance’ with ‘same variable name’ to make it simpler?

No. Matching variable names does not establish that the proposed binder has the required scope relationship to an occurrence. Scope-tree dominance is the stated criterion, and alpha-normalization makes variable spelling especially unsuitable as a substitute for a structural binding check.
Does the plan specify the exact form of the scope tree or a particular binder-type inventory?

No. It names the two filtering criteria but leaves their formal representation and implementation unspecified. Adding a particular tree encoding or list of binder types would introduce details the plan does not provide.
How would you state the plan in one sentence without suggesting the evaluation is already finished?

Generate ScopeBind recombinations, filter them by scope-tree dominance and binder-type compatibility, then compare logical-form exact match on withheld scope–binding combinations and familiar constructions against an equally sized supervised baseline.
Is it important to say that both withheld and familiar figures are exact-match measures?

Yes. The plan specifies exact match for both comparisons. The withheld measure concerns the unseen scope–binding combinations, while the familiar measure concerns constructions whose accuracy the goal seeks to preserve. Neither comparison should be replaced with an unspecified notion of performance.
So the immediate purpose of the plan is to apply the two checks and make both comparisons, while the accuracy thresholds remain targets?

Exactly. Generate the recombinations, filter by scope-tree dominance and binder type, and compare withheld and familiar exact match with the supervised baseline. The ≥90% withheld threshold and the two-percentage-point familiar-accuracy limit remain criteria to assess, not outcomes implied by carrying out the plan.

To evaluate the filtering hypothesis, I want to run three-seed ScopeBind ablations on matched withheld and familiar splits. The comparison would use exact match for dominance/type-filtered recombination, an unfiltered baseline, and a supervised baseline. Is that an accurate description of the activity?

Yes. The activity is to run three-seed ScopeBind ablations on matched withheld/familiar splits and compare exact-match performance for dominance/type-filtered recombination against unfiltered and supervised baselines. It describes an evaluation to run, not results already observed.
What makes this an ablation rather than just a single ScopeBind evaluation?

The filtered-versus-unfiltered comparison examines the presence of the proposed recombination filter. The supervised baseline supplies another comparison point for exact-match accuracy. The activity names these comparisons, but does not specify additional variants.
Does “dominance/type-filtered” mean each recombination has to pass both checks?

That is the intended distinction: the filtered condition applies scope-tree dominance and binder-type compatibility, rather than relying on either condition alone. The activity does not specify separate dominance-only or type-only ablations.
So I should not describe this as isolating the individual contribution of each check?

Correct. Comparing the combined filter with an unfiltered baseline can examine the combined filtering choice. Without separately stated single-check conditions, this activity does not isolate the effect of dominance from the effect of binder-type compatibility.
What does the unfiltered baseline mean in this comparison?

It is the comparison point without the dominance/type filter on recombination. That contrast is relevant to the filtering hypothesis. The activity does not give further specifications for that baseline, so there is no need to infer other differences or detailed construction rules.
And what role does the supervised baseline play?

It provides the supervised reference for the exact-match comparisons. In particular, the established familiar-construction goal compares accuracy with an equally sized supervised baseline. The activity also calls for comparing withheld exact match against a supervised baseline; that comparison is distinct from asking whether withheld accuracy reaches the goal’s absolute threshold.
Why keep the withheld and familiar splits separate in the report of this activity?

They address different parts of the goal. Exact match on withheld scope–binding combinations speaks to generalization, while exact match on familiar constructions speaks to retaining familiar accuracy. A single combined score would not make those two comparisons clear.
What does “matched withheld/familiar splits” commit us to?

It commits the activity to using matched splits for the withheld and familiar evaluation. The established withheld-combination requirement specifies matched vocabulary and length distributions. The activity does not spell out any additional matching procedure or item-by-item correspondence, so it is best not to add one.
Does three-seed mean three different datasets?

No. “Three-seed” specifies repetition across three seeds for the ScopeBind ablations; it does not say there are three different datasets. The activity does not specify which parts of a run the seeds affect or how results across seeds will be summarized.
Should I say that all three comparison conditions use exactly the same seed protocol?

That is not established here. The activity calls for three-seed ScopeBind ablations and comparisons with unfiltered and supervised baselines, but it does not fully specify the seed protocol for every baseline. You can retain the stated three-seed requirement without filling in that detail.
Is exact match the measure for both withheld and familiar performance?

Yes. The activity specifies comparison by exact match on the matched withheld and familiar splits. In the goal, the withheld target is logical-form exact match, and the familiar-construction requirement is also expressed in exact-match accuracy.
How does the activity actually bear on the hypothesis?

It creates a comparison in which the proposed dominance/type-filtered recombination can be examined against unfiltered recombination and a supervised baseline on both kinds of split. The resulting exact-match measurements would be relevant to the hypothesis’s prediction of ≥90% withheld exact match without more than a two-percentage-point familiar-accuracy deficit. The activity itself does not establish either outcome.
If the filtered condition reaches 90% withheld exact match, is that enough to say the hypothesis holds?

Not by itself. The hypothesis also predicts that familiar-construction exact-match accuracy will be no more than two percentage points below the equally sized supervised baseline. Reaching exactly 90% would meet the withheld threshold, but the familiar comparison would still matter.
Does the supervised baseline have to reach 90% on the withheld split?

Can we say what happened on the other seven?
Only that they were not among the 12 exact-form recoveries. This decision does not characterize their remaining errors or say whether their scope collisions persisted.
Is the fallback automatically invoked whenever ScopeBind makes a mistake?

No such mechanism is specified. The decision identifies tagged continuations as a collision fallback; it does not say how a collision would be detected at runtime or prescribe invoking the fallback for every ScopeBind error.
Could I report the primary-plus-fallback system as having a higher withheld exact-match score than 91.2%?
Not from this decision. The 91.2% figure belongs to ScopeBind, and 12/19 measures recoveries within an audited group. There is no measured exact-match score for a combined system here.
What does retaining CCG as a comparator entail?
It keeps the typed CCG approach in a comparison role. The decision does not select it as the primary parser or the collision fallback, and it does not specify a new comparison protocol or result.
Should I call CCG a backup parser?
No. “Comparator” is the stated role. Calling it a backup would assign it a fallback function that this decision gives to tagged continuations for collision cases.
What is being rejected when we say ‘subthreshold fragments’?

Typed-fragment unification is rejected as the primary parser. “Subthreshold” describes the reason relevant to that choice; the decision does not say that fragment-based components are impossible to use in every other capacity.
Does that rejection also apply to the typed CCG chart?

No. The decision treats them separately: typed CCG is retained as a comparator, while subthreshold typed-fragment unification is rejected as the primary parser. They should not be grouped under one label simply because both use types.
Are ScopeBind, tagged continuations, and CCG three interchangeable options in this decision?
No. Their assigned roles differ: ScopeBind is primary, tagged continuations are the collision fallback, and typed CCG is a comparator. Typed-fragment unification is not selected as primary.
Does the recovery finding mean tagged continuations replace ScopeBind on all withheld cases?
No. It is specifically a collision-fallback designation, supported by recoveries among the examined collision-signature failures. Extending that to every withheld case would go beyond the decision.
Can I attribute ScopeBind’s 91.2% to the fallback?
No. The 91.2% is ScopeBind’s own reported withheld exact-match figure. The tagged-continuation recovery count is a separate observation used to support its fallback role.
Is 12/19 a percentage-point improvement over ScopeBind?

No. It is a count of exact-form recoveries within 19 audited collision-signature cases. A percentage-point improvement in full-split accuracy would require a measured comparison on the relevant split, which this decision does not provide.
Does the decision specify a familiar-construction accuracy for the selected arrangement?

No. It states ScopeBind’s 91.2% withheld exact match and the fallback’s 12/19 audited recoveries, but no familiar score for a primary-plus-fallback arrangement. The selection should not be presented as a new measurement of that arrangement’s familiar accuracy.
How narrowly should I describe the evidence for the fallback?

Say that tagged continuations recovered exact logical forms for 12 of 19 examined failures with ScopeTag collision signatures. That preserves the count, its denominator, and the kind of cases involved without implying a guarantee for other collisions.
Does assigning a fallback role prove that a deployed parser can recognize those signatures?

No. The cross-check identified signatures in audited failures, but this decision does not specify a deployment-time signature detector. The role selection and the mechanics of invoking a fallback are distinct.

Select ScopeBind, with 91.2% withheld logical-form exact match, as primary; designate tagged continuations as the collision fallback on the strength of 12/19 exact-form recoveries; retain typed CCG as a comparator; and reject subthreshold typed-fragment unification as the primary parser.
